opus-5.5.text:
I think a few things have come together at once. The first is just raw capability: the models have gotten meaningfully better at reasoning through multi-step problems. A year or two ago, you could ask a model a question and get a good answer, but if you asked it to actually *do* something that took twenty or thirty steps, it would usually go off the rails somewhere in the middle. Now they're much better at holding a goal in mind, checking their own work, and recovering when something goes wrong.

The second piece is that we've started measuring the right things. A lot of my work has been on evaluations, and for a long time the field was focused on benchmarks that looked like exams: multiple choice, short answers, academic questions. Those are useful, but they don't tell you whether a model can actually help someone get their job done. When you start building evals around real tasks, the kind of work people actually do on a computer every day, you get a much clearer signal about where models are genuinely useful and where they still fall short. That feedback loop has helped push progress in a more practical direction.

And the third thing is the tooling around the models. Giving them the ability to use a browser, write and run code, work with files, and operate in a real environment changes what's possible. It's the difference between a very smart person you can only talk to on the phone versus someone who can actually sit down at your computer and help.

So when you put those together, better reasoning, better measurement of real-world tasks, and the ability to act, you cross a threshold where it stops being a neat demo and starts being something people reach for every day. It's not perfect, there are still plenty of tasks where models struggle, but the slope of improvement has been really striking, and I think a lot of people are feeling that in their own work now.

r003.rationale: It describes a practical-usefulness threshold, but does not define it as delegation taking less time than doing the task oneself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the simplest way to put it is that for a long time, models were good at answering questions, and now they're actually good at doing things. Those sound similar, but they're really different problems. Answering a question is one shot: you read the input, you produce an output, you're done. Doing a task on a computer means you have to look at a screen, decide what to click, type something, see what happened, realize you made a mistake, back up, try again. It's a long chain of small decisions, and if any one of them goes wrong early, the whole thing can fall apart.

What changed, in my view, is a few things coming together at once. The models got much better at perception, so they can actually read a messy spreadsheet or a web form or a terminal and understand what's in front of them. They got better at planning over longer horizons, so they can hold a goal in mind across dozens of steps instead of losing the thread. And reliability went up a lot. That last one matters more than people appreciate. If a model gets each step right ninety percent of the time, a twenty-step task almost never succeeds. If it gets each step right ninety-nine percent of the time, suddenly it mostly works. We crossed that threshold on a lot of ordinary tasks, and it feels like a phase change even though under the hood it was gradual improvement.

The other piece is that we started measuring the right things. Early on, benchmarks were mostly trivia and puzzles. Those are useful, but they don't tell you whether a model can file an expense report or clean up a dataset or reconcile two calendars. Once we started building evals that looked like real work, with real software and real failure modes, we could see exactly where models were breaking and fix it. So the usefulness you feel today is partly capability and partly that the whole field got much more honest about what "useful" actually means.

And honestly, part of the tipping point is just that people are trying it. For a while even people who worked on this stuff didn't hand the model a real task and walk away. Now they do, and it works often enough that you start to rebuild your habits around it. That's the real sign to me. Not a benchmark number, but people quietly changing how they get through their day.

r002.rationale: It does not identify high latency as a barrier or refer to earlier agents such as Operator or ChatGPT agent.

r003.rationale: It describes a tipping point in task reliability and adoption, but does not locate it at AI delegation becoming faster than doing the task oneself.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at a point where models can move beyond answering questions to actually helping you get things done. A lot of everyday computer tasks sound simple—finding information, comparing options, filling out a form—but they require understanding what’s on a screen, deciding what to do next, and adjusting when something unexpected happens.

As those capabilities come together, you can start describing the outcome you want instead of specifying every click. The model still needs to be reliable and know when to ask for your input, but that shift—from giving you advice to carrying out useful steps—is what makes this feel like a tipping point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s the combination of models getting better at understanding what you want and getting better at taking the steps to actually do it. A lot of everyday computer tasks sound simple—find some information, compare a few options, put the results in a spreadsheet—but they require you to move between tools, keep track of context, and handle things that don’t go exactly as expected.

As models get better at that, the interaction starts to change. You can describe the outcome you want instead of spelling out every click. There’s still work to do on reliability, but being able to delegate a useful chunk of a task is a pretty meaningful shift.
